main_point.en: We can look to Jesus’s works to settle our doubts.

christ_connection.en: When Jesus answered John the Baptist’s question, He pointed to miracles only the Messiah would have authority to do. Jesus would later demonstrate His authority over sin and evil in a greater way through His crucifixion and resurrection. While many continue to reject Him, one day every knee will bow and every tongue confess He is Lord (Phil. 2:9-11).

content.en:
1 When Jesus had finished instructing his twelve disciples, he went on from there to teach and preach in their cities. 
2 Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Christ, he sent word by his disciples 
3 and said to him, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” 
4 And Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: 
5 the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them. 
6 And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” 
7 As they went away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? 
8 What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses. 
9 What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. 
10 This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’”

11 “Truly, I say to you, among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. 
12 From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has suffered violence, and the violent take it by force. 
13 For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John, 
14 and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah who is to come. 
15 He who has ears to hear, let him hear. 
16 But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their playmates, 
17 ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’ 
18 For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ 
19 The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.”
Leaders: Our God isn’t offended by our questions. Instead, He shows us compassion when we bring Him our doubts in an effort to know Him more deeply.

“Interestingly, the passages that Jesus alluded to in Isaiah refer not only to healing but also to the judgment that the Messiah would bring. Jesus’s miraculous works were evidence of the inbreaking kingdom; therefore John needed to trust that Jesus would indeed bring full and final judgment, a judgment that comes to the fore in verses 20-24. God will be true to His Word, and to try to fight doubt without a foundation in the truth of His Word is futile. God’s Word is a rock, not because it makes everything easy, but because it keeps your feet out of sinking sand amid difficult situations and unmet expectations.”¹

“In the entirety of the Old Testament, no blind person ever received sight, nor is there any story in the New Testament, apart from Saul’s conversion (Acts 9:17-18), where Jesus’s followers restored a blind man’s sight. Jesus was fulfilling what Isaiah had long ago prophesied, ‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened’ (35:5).”²

“We probably tend to underestimate the extent to which Jesus entered into joyous table-fellowship with people who had known only exclusion but who now knew the joy of forgiveness and acceptance. This was the background to the koinonia so important to the early church. It foreshadowed the Lord’s Supper and the ultimate ‘messianic banquet’ (Acts 2:42; Rev. 3:20). This table-fellowship with such people probably more than anything else aroused the wrath of the Pharisees.”³

John the Baptist and many other Jews wanted to know for sure that Jesus was the Messiah. Before we can understand their confusion and questions, we have to understand what the word “Messiah” would’ve meant to them. Messiah (or in the Greek, Christos; where we get the title “Christ”) means “anointed one.” The idea of anointing appears repeatedly throughout the Old Testament. Yahweh the Lord) anointed people, or approved them for special roles or positions. Most often, anointed ones represented God and delivered His words to His people. God anointed priests, prophets, and kings—even pagan kings—to carry out the tasks He’d planned for them (Rom. 13:1). But the Messiah was a special prophesied deliverer, who would come from the line of King David. People expected Him to come as a warrior prince, who would overthrow the Romans and establish His own kingdom on earth—a kingdom where the Jews would rise above all their oppressors. However, the people missed that though the Messiah was a prophesied deliverer from oppression, He was also the prophesied deliverer from sin and its effects on the world. Jesus redirected John’s attention to this truth. Jesus was doing exactly what prophecy said the Messiah would do: healing, sharing the good news, and setting people free.

Because of the vast difference between God’s wisdom and ours and because of humanity’s sinful state, human beings are incapable, on our own, of fully grasping spiritual truth without being aided by the Holy Spirit through the process of illumination. When it comes to applying the meaning of God’s Word, Christians do not rely ultimately on human reason in the process of interpretation, nor do we rely solely on an institution or body of scholars. Instead, a Christian’s ultimate reliance is on the work of the Holy Spirit, who illuminates the Scriptures in the heart and mind (John 14:15-18; 16:7-15).

GOD, TURN OUR ATTENTION TO YOU WHEN WE WRESTLE WITH DOUBTS. REMIND US OF THE WORK YOU’VE DONE IN THE PAST THAT REVEALS YOUR FAITHFULNESS. HELP US TO USE THESE EXPERIENCES TO ENCOURAGE OUR STUDENTS THAT THEY’RE NOT ALONE IN THEIR QUESTIONS OR IN THEIR DESIRE TO BE SURE OF WHAT THEY BELIEVE.

DID YOU KNOW? Many people struggle with imposter syndrome—extreme self-doubt or feeling fake, even if they actually know what they’re doing. But some people suffer from the opposite, the Dunning-Kruger effect. They overestimate their abilities and lack enough awareness of their flaws to grow.⁴

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You'll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for students to connect more to the lesson as they connect to the topic and to one another.

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: When have you doubted someone’s story?
How can you tell when someone is lying? What do you look or listen for?
What would you do if you suspected someone you trusted wasn’t telling the truth about something important to you?

content.en: We've all heard stories that sounded unbelievable. Our minds constantly scan the words people say, their facial expressions, and their body language to help us know if they’re being real. Doubts are a very normal part of our lives. But doubts aren’t always bad; they can actually lead us to ask questions that strengthen our faith and draw us closer to Jesus.

cultural_connection.en: Where do you go with your doubts? When we scroll social media, we can find influencers for almost anything. If we aren’t careful, reels and stories can convince us that these people have all the answers we could ever need. Sometimes, other people do have answers we need and can help us make wise choices. But unless we truly know the people behind the accounts, it’s impossible to trust completely that they are exactly who they appear to be. That’s not to say we can’t be inspired by something they say or learn something new from them—we definitely can! However, when it comes to doubts about our faith, about Jesus, we need to make sure we’re taking our questions to the right places and holding up the answers against the truth of God’s Word. While going to godly, trustworthy people with our doubts or questions isn’t wrong, Jesus should always be our starting point—just like He was for John the Baptist.

question.en: John prophesied about Jesus as the One who would take away sin, so what do you think made him doubt?

answer.en: Leaders: See context note on Messiah. As the prophet who’d prepared the way for Jesus’s ministry, John had every reason to believe Jesus was who He claimed to be (John 1:29-34). But Jesus wasn’t doing what John expected: He wasn’t overthrowing Rome; He was hanging out with “tax collectors and sinners” (v. 19). John also wasn’t in the best situation: He was in prison for calling out King Herod’s sin. Doubt often comes to us when we’re struggling with the weight of unmet expectations or a difficult situation. Like John, we might wonder: “Is Jesus really who I thought He was?” But the truth is: He’s even better.

question.en: What evidence did Jesus give John to prove He is who He claims to be?

answer.en: When John questioned Jesus’s identity as the Messiah, Jesus didn’t snap back or ignore John’s disciples. Instead, Jesus answered them plainly, pointing to specific events in His ministry, like healing the sick and sharing the good news of the gospel. The evidence Jesus gave John fulfilled prophecy from the book of Isaiah—prophecy John would’ve known. Jesus both reassured John of His identity and shifted John’s attention away from promises of judgment and toward promises of salvation. When we have questions and doubts, we can turn our attention to God’s Word and find the answers we need.

question.en: When is it difficult to battle doubt? How does it comfort you to know Jesus meets us where we are, even when we doubt?

answer.en: We can imagine that John’s time in prison was filled with dark, depressing days. John desperately needed hope, and despite his doubt, he reached out to the one Person he knew could give it. Jesus met John there in his doubt, and He’ll do the same for us. We may wrestle with doubt when we face sickness, the death of someone we love, friends betraying us, or uncertainty about the future. But when we feel overwhelmed by life or don’t know when the pressure will let up, we can run to Jesus and trust Him to help us. He doesn’t reject us or put us down when we come to Him with our doubting hearts; He invites us close and promises we’ll find rest (Matt. 11:29-30). We often attempt to hide our doubt or stuff our questions down deep, maybe because we fear God’s response. But through the life of Jesus, we see the Father’s heart for us. We can trust Him with our questions.

question.en: What advantages do we have now to strengthen our faith that John didn’t have?

answer.en: Jesus knew what was coming, but John could only see what was happening in the moment. We weren’t made to hold it all or know everything. Our perspective (and John’s) is limited. We only know what we can see and understand, but God is greater than us, and His plans are greater too. We have two advantages John didn’t have: We can see the rest of Jesus’s ministry, death, and resurrection on the pages of Scripture. And when we trust in Him as Savior, we receive the Holy Spirit, who helps us know and trust that Jesus is who He claims to be.

question.en: What does it mean that Jesus was “a friend of ... sinners” (v. 19)? How does that compare to the way people think of Jesus today?

answer.en: The Jews called Jesus “a friend of ... sinners” as an insult because they pictured their Messiah as a conquering king who didn’t associate with the lowly. But to us, these words are grace: We are all sinners in need of a Friend who loved us enough to lay down His life to free us from our sin. Jesus went to people who’d only ever known life as outsiders—and He invited them in. Despite what many people might believe today, Jesus doesn’t reject us because of what we’ve done; He invites us in to experience freedom from sin because of what He has done for us.

question.en: What’s the difference in John’s doubt and the Jews’ unbelief Jesus called out in verses 16-17?

answer.en: Jesus called out the Jews by comparing them to children who only wanted to play a game if they could do it their way. In other words, the Jews refused to believe in Jesus or the words of John the Baptist because Jesus wasn’t the Messiah they wanted or expected—a powerful ruler and conqueror. Unbelief comes from a lack of faith, a complete rejection of Jesus and His way of life. Faith is trusting what we can’t see (Heb. 11:1), and doubt is acknowledging our desire to be sure we’re trusting the right idea or person. John’s question teaches us that we’re not alone when we struggle with doubt and that doubt doesn’t mean we lack faith. Unbelief, however, separates us from God because it’s the choice to reject what we’ve seen and heard about Jesus. But if we turn to Jesus with our questions, like John, doubt can draw us closer to Jesus instead.

question.en: Jesus is the friend of sinners. How can we imitate Him while also keeping ourselves from falling into sin?

answer.en: The Jews called out Jesus for hanging out with sinners as if it was a bad thing. But Jesus knew His mission, and He based His ministry around it: He came to give hope to those who were lost and hurting and who recognized their need for something more. Jesus could hang out with people who didn’t live like Him without fear that their words and actions would draw Him into sin. But He still shows us how to be friends to sinners without falling into sin: We ground ourselves in our identity as children of God, recharge by spending time in God’s presence, learn Scripture so we can stand firm on God’s Word when someone challenges us, and surround ourselves with close friends who follow Jesus and can hold us accountable to do the same. These practices build a solid spiritual support system for us, a safe place where we can return again and again to find rest, truth, and restoration as we go out into the world to invite the lost and hurting to come and see Jesus.

content.en:
Have you ever heard something that sounded mostly good and right but just slightly off? We shrug off our doubt because we’re busy, rushed, or pressured to go along with what the rest of our family or friends decide or to trust the person who’s advising us. Doubt can be good for you, though: It’s that little catch in your breath, stumbling step, glance over your shoulder, or check in your spirit that makes you pause and wonder if you’re going the right way. Doubt makes us pause and ask, “Is what I’m feeling or experiencing actually real or true?”

The enemy would like nothing more than to make you doubt what God has said and to turn away from His Word toward something that sounds good and justifies your ideas or desires. We like to think that Satan’s tactics are obvious, but it’s not so simple. In fact, sin entered the world because the enemy is smart and sneaky and twists God’s words so that we begin to wonder if we heard Him correctly. Whether his question to us is as plainly stated as it was to Eve, the enemy can tempt us to wonder, “Did God actually say .. . ?” (v. 1; emphasis added).

Faced with the serpent’s question, Eve chose to allow doubt to drive a wedge between her and God. We easily do the same when our desires—or culture’s opinions—don’t line up with what God has actually said. But when we’re faced with influencers’ messages, friends’ opinions, or even teachers’ lessons that cause us to wonder what God has really said, we can let our questions be invitations to press deeper into our relationship with Jesus, asking the Holy Spirit for guidance as we look to God’s Word to see what’s true. Then, we walk toward that truth instead of falling for the enemy’s same old schemes.

Lord Jesus, sometimes I struggle to know what’s from You and what’s from the world and just sounds right. Help me to listen to the Holy Spirit and remember Your Word so I can know Your way in all things.

question.en: God will never ask you to do something that doesn’t line up with His Word. How can this help you tell what’s true?
What are some ways you can build spiritual defenses now so you can stand against the enemy’s lies when they come?

prayer.en: Lord Jesus, sometimes I struggle to know what’s from You and what’s from the world and just sounds right. Help me to listen to the Holy Spirit and remember Your Word so I can know Your way in all things.

content.en:
Maybe you've heard of “The Five Ws” (and One H) of writing. They break down like this: “Who” points to the people involved. “What” tells us about the plot or events. “When” alerts us to the time. “Where” indicates location. “Why” explains the reason behind an action. “How” describes the process. Asking all of these questions gives us a clear picture, a full story. They help us learn and discover, and they can also help us settle our doubts.

In faith, like in writing, we start with the first question to help us settle our doubts: who. God ultimately holds all the answers. When we ask what we know about Him, we can answer that He is holy, righteous, good, loving, just, and merciful—just to name a few of His attributes. When and where tell us that He always has been and always will be everywhere across all times and with all people. But the hows and whys of faith are far more mysterious to us. We can only know what God decides to reveal when He decides to reveal it because the way He thinks and works in the world is so far beyond our ability to understand.

This is why faith, trusting what we can’t see or understand, is necessary in our relationship with God. When we don’t understand, we can trust God does. When we have doubts, we can trust that He is sure and steady. When we have questions, we can trust that He has answers, even if they aren’t what we hoped for. Though God never promises that we will understand everything He does or the reasons behind those actions, He promises that when we search for Him, we will find Him (Jer. 29:13). And ultimately, He is the answer we need.

question.en: What’s going on in your life right now that you don’t understand? What questions do you have for God?
How do you think going to God with your questions could strengthen your faith?

prayer.en: GOD, HELP ME TO TRUST YOU EVEN THOUGH I WON’T ALWAYS BE ABLE TO SEE OR UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU’RE DOING OR WHY YOU ALLOW CERTAIN THINGS TO HAPPEN. GUIDE ME TO ASK QUESTIONS THAT GROW MY FAITH, NOT INCREASE MY DOUBT.

content.en:
We all have friends or people in our lives who are our “go-tos” for certain things. Maybe your artsy friend helps you decorate for another friend’s birthday party. Maybe you ask your mom for help with homework because she’s really good at math. Maybe your older brother plays guitar, so you ask him to help you write and perform a song. Beyond your everyday needs, though, you probably trust specific people to help you meet specialized needs, like a dentist who helps you with a toothache or a tutor who helps you prepare for the SAT. We all need help sometimes, and who we turn to matters.

The Gospels make it clear that Jesus is the go-to for people in need. He healed the sick, cast out demons, and even raised the dead. His work had caught the attention of a desperate father who wanted help for his demon-possessed son. This man sought Jesus with confidence, but doubt crept in when the disciples failed to help. When Jesus arrived and said He could help if the man believed, the man cried out with a desperate plea many of us can identify with: “I believe; help my unbelief” (v. 24).

It’s like saying, “Jesus, I trust you, and deep down, I know you can help. But nothing else has worked, and everyone else failed, so I’m also struggling with doubt. Help me to trust you completely.” When you do this, you’re not saying you don’t believe in Jesus’s power to heal or help you; you're admitting that you’re human, flawed, and in need of your perfect Savior to remind you once again that He is faithful to do what He has promised. So, when you’re struggling with doubt, ask Jesus for help.

question.en: When have you felt the tension of knowing you can trust Jesus and experiencing doubt because your situation seems impossible?
How can Jesus doing what seemed impossible in the past give you confidence that He can do the impossible now?

prayer.en: GOD, THANK YOU FOR HEARING ME AND HELPING ME, EVEN WHEN MY FAITH IS SMALL. I BELIEVE YOU CAN HELP ME AND WILL DO ALL YOU’VE PROMISED. EVEN WHEN I DOUBT, GIVE ME STRENGTH TO TRUST YOU FULLY.

content.en:
Despite living in the age of social media and phones with amazing cameras, most of us have probably had that moment when we realized we should’ve taken more pictures. Not just any pictures though—not the aesthetic latte art, the beautiful sunset, or the new car. No, the moments we want to hold on to most are milestone events and the people who make our lives so amazing. But pictures aren’t the only way we remember. We remember through stories, souvenirs, and monuments too. Remembering is an important part of life. Memories help us learn new information, organize ideas, and even make plans for the future. Basically, looking back helps us look forward.

God encouraged His people toward specific ways of remembering because they were forgetful. So, they celebrated through feasts and festivals, gifts and sacrifices, songs and Scripture readings—and even through stones. When God’s people finally crossed the Jordan River before entering the promised land, the priests carried the ark of the covenant to the middle of the river as God had commanded, and God held back the waters so the people could cross. Here, God instructed Joshua to choose one man from each tribe to gather stones from the riverbed. Then, Joshua commanded the men to carry the stones and to set them down where they spent the night. These stones were meant to serve as a memorial to God’s faithfulness (v. 7).

Like the Israelites, we need to remember—and keep remembering—how God has been faithful to us. In our moments of doubt, these memorials can settle our hearts. When we remember the works God has done, we can rest, knowing He will do everything He said He would do. We can look back at God’s faithfulness to look ahead in faith.

question.en: What are some practical ways you remember important moments or people?
How can you remember what God has done for you? How can you create your own stones of remembrance?

prayer.en: HEAVENLY FATHER, I KNOW I’M FORGETFUL. BRING TO MIND THE TIMES YOU’VE SHOWN ME WHO YOU ARE AND HOW YOU LOVE ME. TEACH ME HOW TO CREATE MY OWN MEMORIALS OF YOUR FAITHFULNESS TO KEEP ME FROM FORGETTING.

content.en:
Think about the most unbelievable story you’ve ever heard or the most unbelievable story you’ve lived through. No matter the teller, the more unbelievable the story, the more likely those listening will want proof. Sometimes, we can easily see a photo or a scar, pull up a news story, or ask family members or friends to act as witnesses to the truth of their tales. Sometimes, we see evidence in the way people’s thoughts, words, and behaviors change. Other times, we have to believe what they say is true because we know and trust their character.

Before Jesus came, people like Abraham, Moses, and King David had faith that God would one day send the King He had promised and establish His eternal kingdom, but they died without seeing that promise fulfilled. They were approved by this belief, this complete trust, in what God would do, despite not seeing the total fulfillment of the promise (Heb. 11:2,39). They believed because they saw God work miraculously in and through His people—including themselves—to conquer kingdoms, build temples, stand firm in their faith despite persecution, wander the wilderness, see the dead raised to life (Heb. 11:35), and countless other acts throughout their history.

Unlike these heroes of the faith, we know Jesus came and have the privilege of looking back at God’s promises fulfilled. Believers are assured of this reality through Scripture and the presence of the Holy Spirit living within us as a holy, eternal promise. And yet, when we struggle with doubt, like those heroes of the faith, we can also see the way God has worked in the lives of others—and worked within us—as evidence that He is who He says He is and will do what He has promised.

question.en: Whose life shows evidence that God has changed him or her? What evidence do you see?
Does your life give enough evidence for people around you to believe Jesus is who He says He is? Explain.

prayer.en: Lord Jesus, I want to live life Your way so that people see evidence of Your presence in my words and actions. Help me to view good works as evidence to help others know You, not as acts to make myself look good.
